children: Canadian manufacturing activity softened again last month, with the industry continuing to notch a lift in production in the face of a fall in new orders and a spike in cost inflation, data showed Thursday.

The S&P Global Canada manufacturing purchasing managers index eased to 51.5 in September, the lowest reading since March and a signal of only modest growth. The index has been above the 50 threshold between expansion and contraction for six months running, after dipping to 53 in August.
"Canada's manufacturing economy showed a degree of resilience in the face of several headwinds during September," Paul Smith, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said.
Businesses and households in Canada have been hit with fresh uncertainty amid heightened trade tensions between Ottawa and Washington and as oil prices remain high.

Manufacturing output rose and companies showed a willingness to fill vacancies with skilled workers to support recent long-term contracts. However, tariffs and elevated global energy prices due to the war in Iran continued to have a damaging impact on the sector, Smith said.

While output continued to rise in September, it was at the slowest pace in the past six months as new orders declined marginally for the first time since March, S&P Global's survey showed. Manufacturers noted a degree of client hesitancy, largely due to tariffs, which were reported to have negatively impacted international demand, especially among clients based in the U.S.

Customs delays and U.S. border difficulties, plus the Iran war and demand related to artificial-intelligence infrastructure buildouts, were all reported to have added strain on already stretched supply chains, S&P Global said.

Vendors were again reported to be short of stock, and there were reports of container-shipping delays on key maritime routes. Delivery delays were the most widespread since August 2022, which led companies to use existing inventory wherever possible.

Widespread product shortages and elevated fuel prices contributed to a jump in input costs, with inflation overall at the highest recorded by the survey since mid-2022. The poll found that manufacturers responded by increasing their own charges, though some firms reported that a weak demand environment had limited their pricing power.

Confidence in the outlook for manufacturing in Canada dropped to its lowest level since last December, though companies continued to add to their workforce numbers, with employment increasing overall for a sixth consecutive month.

Canada's economy is expected to have cooled in the third quarter after a strong rebound the quarter before. Industry-level gross domestic product was flat in July, snapping three straight months of expansion. Early data points to growth of 0.2% in August from the month before, with a recovery in mining and retail trade that was partially offset by further declines in oil-and-gas extraction.

The Trump administration in August imposed new 50% tariffs on the equivalent of about 5% of Canadian exported goods, and then in September the president signed orders to ban the importation of many dairy products, alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada in response to retaliatory Canadian tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods.
